reference_action: OP confirmed improved after advice to water more; answer corrected Yucca identification to Dracaena marginata and identified shriveling from underwatering.

actions.action: Sterilize saw and cut healthy top
Check soil to bottom before watering

resolved.reason: Treats the mislabeled Dracaena as desert Yucca, dismisses underwatering, and emphasizes drying/rot rescue. This may prolong the demonstrated dehydration; conditional deep watering does not outweigh opposite-direction guidance.

harmfulness.reason: “Almost impossible” to kill by underwatering and the extra-cup warning discourage needed hydration. Strong sun and conditional cutting also risk worsening a stressed, misidentified plant.

specificity_accuracy.reason: Uses the user’s incorrect Yucca label and attributes droop to light or rot. It misses the shriveled-stem dehydration that improved with watering.

feasibility.reason: Moisture and stem checks are concrete. Sawing, callusing, mineral-mix repotting and multiple care adjustments add work beyond the required simple intervention.

sources.reason: Explicitly dismisses underwatering and requires complete drying; drenching is conditional in the opposite-direction regimen.
Bottom watering every 7–10 days gives a concrete hydration action, although fixed ounces and wrong Yucca assumptions reduce suitability. Partial action overlap, not diagnostic correctness.
Post-repot support/sun/patience and longer watering intervals, not increased hydration.
Advice explicitly says watering too much and extends intervals to 3–6 weeks. A drench within that reduced-watering regimen is not equivalent to correcting dehydration here.
Second answer says give plenty of water in spring/summer; partial hydration overlap despite inappropriate outdoor Yucca context and cutting advice elsewhere.

[0:00] The yucca cane is one of the most resilient, architectural, and beautiful
[0:03] desert giants you can grow in your living room. In our greenhouse, these
[0:07] trees are legendary because they can thrive on neglect and survive weeks
[0:11] without a single drop of water. But in a home environment, a silent killer often
[0:16] strikes. Indoor growers treat them like tropical plants, watering them too often
[0:21] until the leaves turn yellow or brown, the foliage starts drooping, and the
[0:25] hard, woody trunk becomes soft, mushy, and hollow. If your yucca is showing any
[0:30] of these scary symptoms, do not panic. Today, I am going to share the top three
[0:35] greenhouse secrets we use to diagnose yucca problems instantly, keep trunks
[0:39] rock solid, and save a rotting tree, even if you think it's completely dead.
[0:44] Let's start with the most dangerous symptom, a soft, spongy trunk. Because
[0:48] yucca trees store all their water inside their thick canes, root rot travels
[0:52] upward from the soil inside the wood, completely invisible from the outside.
[0:56] To catch this early, you must physically squeeze the bottom of the trunk with
[1:00] your fingers every single month. If it feels hard like stone, your tree is
[1:04] safe. But if it feels soft or if the bark is peeling away,
[1:09] the inside of that cane is already rotting from overwatering. In our
[1:12] nursery, if we catch a soft trunk, we immediately stop watering and take the
[1:16] plant out of its pot. If the rot is only at the base, you can actually use a
[1:20] clean, sterilized saw to cut the top, healthy, hard part of the cane. Let it
[1:25] dry for 2 days to callus and repot it in fresh soil. It will grow brand new
[1:29] roots, saving your beloved tree from the trash can.
[1:32] The second major issue is droopy, floppy leaves. Healthy yucca leaves should
[1:37] stand stiff and point upward like swords. If your plant's leaves are
[1:41] bending downward and losing their firmness,
[1:44] it is a direct sign of light starvation. Yucca plants are native to the hot, arid
[1:50] deserts of Mexico and the southwestern United States, meaning they are
[1:53] biologically wired for intense, direct sunlight. When placed in a dim corner of
[1:58] a living room, their metabolism drops to zero. In a dark room, the plant stops
[2:02] drinking, which keeps the soil wet for weeks and instantly triggers root rot.
[2:07] To fix droopy leaves at home, your yucca must be placed right against your
[2:10] brightest south or west-facing window. Give it the desert light it craves, and
[2:15] the new growth will emerge stiff and strong. Now, let's decode yellow and
[2:19] brown leaves. The golden rule of yucca care is very simple. When in doubt, do
[2:25] not water. It is almost impossible to kill a yucca from underwatering, but one
[2:29] extra cup of water can destroy it. In our greenhouse, we let the soil dry out
[2:34] 100% all the way to the bottom of the pot before we even think about watering.
[2:39] At home, use a long wooden stick or a moisture meter to check the very bottom
[2:43] of the pot. If there is even a hint of moisture,
[2:46] walk away. When it is finally bone dry, drench it heavily until water runs out
[2:51] of the drainage holes. But, remember, your soil mix must be desert-like. We
[2:56] use 50% regular potting soil mixed with 50% coarse sand, pumice, and perlite. If
[3:02] your soil retains water like a wet sponge, your yucca is on a countdown to
[3:06] decay. Here is a bonus greenhouse tip for yellow and brown lower leaves. As a
[3:11] yucca tree grows taller from the top, it naturally sheds its lowest leaves to
[3:14] form its woody trunk over time. This is a completely normal aging process. When
[3:19] these bottom leaves turn yellow or brown, take a clean pair of scissors and
[3:23] trim them away. But, here is the secret. Do not rip them off forcefully, as this
[3:28] can tear the delicate bark of the trunk and open up entry wounds for pests. Cut
[3:32] them clean at the base. This keeps your tree looking neat and prevents any pests
[3:36] or fungus from hiding inside the dead foliage. Squeeze the bottom of that
